unit.title: Shares
unit.description: What you buy with a share, how you get dividends and what kinds of companies there are

texts: The general meeting
Pablo
I've got 50 shares and I've received the notice for the general meeting.
They're voting on a big pay rise for the CEO. Whatever, my vote doesn't count…
What do you tell Pablo?
Read the proposal and vote remotely or appoint a proxy
Exactly. It's his right as an owner, and meetings add up big and small votes alike.
Do nothing: with 50 shares it makes no difference
His vote carries little weight, but it counts. If he doesn't vote, others decide for him.
Sell everything in protest
He can, but he gives up his stake without having used his voice.
As a general rule, **one share = one vote**. The big funds really do swing votes.
Your rights
Being a shareholder gives you three kinds of rights, in proportion to your shares.
Economic
Voting
Information
Receiving the dividend if one is paid
That's an economic right: your share of the profit paid out.
Your share if the company is sold or wound up
Another economic right: you get whatever matches your shares.
Voting at the annual general meeting
That's a voting right: you decide with your vote.
Voting on directors' pay
It's voted on at the general meeting: a voting right.
Receiving the annual accounts
That's an information right.
Getting relevant information at the same time as everyone else
Listed companies report it to the CNMV so that everyone learns about it at once.
Sort the six rights.
**Economic**, **voting** and **information** rights. And a very useful one: **pre-emptive rights**, to buy before anyone else in a capital increase so you don't lose your percentage.
Hint: getting paid is economic, having a say is voting, and knowing is information.
You have more rights than it seems.
Tap each right: what kind is it?

steps.title: Information for everyone at once
steps.body:
Listed companies must publish their accounts and report any **inside information** (results, acquisitions, problems) to the **CNMV** so that all investors learn about it at the same time. The accounts of every Spanish listed company are free on the CNMV website.

Some companies have **non-voting** shares or give double votes to people who hold them for years.
steps.key: Being a shareholder gives you economic, voting and information rights, in proportion to your shares.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, add three companies you'd like to own to your Favourites.

u8l3.title: Dividends: how and when you get paid

texts: The master plan
Leo
Plan: I buy at €20 just before the dividend, collect €0.50 and sell.
Free money!
What's wrong with Leo's plan?
Nothing: it's free money
On the day the dividend is deducted, the share opens at around €19.50.
The price drops by roughly what he collects
Exactly. He has €0.50 in cash and €0.50 less in shares.
He has to wait for the payment date
He'll get paid that day, yes. But the price will already have dropped by about €0.50.
Well, at least I get the dividend, right?
And it's taxed: in Spain the payer already **withholds 19 %**.
Do you get the dividend?
From the **ex-dividend date**, the share trades without the right to that dividend. To get it, you need to hold it **before** then.
You get it
You don't get it
You buy two days before the ex-dividend date
You hold it before the ex-dividend date: you get it.
You buy the day before the ex-dividend date
That's the last day to buy and still get paid.
You buy on the ex-dividend date itself
That day it's already trading without the right to that dividend.
You buy on the payment date
Too late: they've already checked who the shareholders were on the record date.
You've held it for a year and sell it on the ex-dividend date
You held it before the ex-dividend date: that dividend is yours.
Decide on all five cases.
The order is **announcement, ex-dividend, record and payment**. To get it, the share has to be yours **by the day before the ex-dividend date at the latest**.
Hint: all that matters is holding it before the ex-dividend date.
The key date isn't the payment date, it's the ex-dividend date.
Do you get it or not? Tap each case

steps.title: Dividend yield
steps.body:
**Dividend yield = annual dividend ÷ price.** A €30 share that pays €1.20 a year yields 4 %.

Careful: a sky-high dividend is sometimes a warning that the price has fallen because a cut is expected.
steps.key: A dividend isn't free money: it comes out of the company's value.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Iberdrola, which pays a dividend every year, and add it to your Favourites.

u8l4.title: Splits, reverse splits and capital increases

texts: «It's dropped 90 %»
Marta
Help! My share has dropped 90 % today.
I had 5 shares… and now it says I've got 50.
What's happened?
She's lost 90 % of her money
She has ten times as many shares, at a tenth of the price: the same.
There's been a 10-for-1 split
Exactly. Same pizza, cut into more slices: her money is worth the same.
The company has given her 45 free shares
It's not a gift: each one is worth a tenth. It's a **split**.
Phew. So why do they do it?
To make each share more manageable. NVIDIA did a 10-for-1 in 2024.
What's happened here?
Three operations that change the number of shares. Only one brings **new money** into the company.
Split
Reverse split
Capital increase
Your 10 shares at €400 become 40 at €100
More slices, same value: you still have €4,000.
Your 1,000 shares at €0.20 become 100 at €2
They're combined: fewer, pricier shares, same value.
The company issues new shares to raise money
New money and more owners come in.
Apple splits each share into four (2020)
A 4-for-1 split: four times as many shares, at a quarter of the price.
A company trading at a few cents combines its shares
Usually done after a big fall: it changes the price, not the value.
If you don't buy, your percentage of the company falls
That's **dilution**: there are more shares and you still have the same number.
Sort the six cases.
Splits and reverse splits only change the number of slices. A **capital increase** does change the cake: new money and more owners come in, and if you don't take part, **you get diluted**.
Hint: does new money come into the company, or is it just sliced differently?
Cutting the pizza into more slices doesn't give you more pizza.
Tap each case: split, reverse split or capital increase?

steps.title: What changes and what doesn't
steps.body:
In a capital increase, **pre-emptive rights** let you buy the new shares you're entitled to before anyone else: that way you keep your percentage.

Some Spanish companies pay the dividend in new shares if you want: the *scrip* or flexible dividend.

If a headline says «the share plunges 75 %», check first whether there's been a split.
steps.key: Splits and reverse splits don't change what you own; a capital increase you don't take part in does: it dilutes you.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for NVIDIA, which did a 10×1 split in 2024, and look at its chart in monthly candles.

texts: The forum micro cap
Ana
On a forum they say this micro cap, a tiny company, could multiply by 10.
I'm putting in all my savings. I'm betting everything on this one!
What do you tell Ana?
Small caps always go up more
Sometimes they rise more, but many fall by the wayside or go bust.
She could lose almost everything: better not to bet it all on one
Exactly. The potential is real, but the risk of a single small company is huge.
Invest only half
That's still a lot in a single small, illiquid company.
Careful: forums are also the favourite hangout of people trying to pump up a share.
Big or small?
**Market cap = price × number of shares**: what the company is worth on the stock market. Its profile changes with its size.
More typical of a large cap
More typical of a small cap
It can multiply in size several times over
A 500 million company can multiply; a giant, hardly.
Hundreds of analysts follow it
The big ones are watched by the whole market.
Wider spreads
There are fewer buyers and sellers: trading costs more.
A more stable price
Large caps tend to be less volatile.
It goes bust more often
Small caps are more fragile: they go bust more often.
It's in the S&P 500 or the IBEX 35
Those are indices of large companies.
It's in the Russell 2000
The Russell 2000 brings together small US companies.
Sort the seven traits.
Smaller = **more potential**, but also **more volatility, less liquidity and more risk of going bust**. Large caps are more stable and hundreds of analysts follow them.
Hint: small things grow faster, but break more easily.
Potential and risk always come together.
Tap each trait: large or small?

steps.title: Sizes and indices
steps.body:
A common convention (in dollars):
• **Large caps:** over 10,000 million.
• **Mid caps:** from 2,000 to 10,000 million.
• **Small caps:** from 300 to 2,000 million.
• Below that, *micro caps*.

In Spain there are the IBEX Medium Cap and IBEX Small Cap. A global index is cap-weighted: the giants weigh most.
steps.key: Smaller = more potential, but also more volatility and more risk of going bust.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare the chart of SXR8, large US companies, with that of IUSN, small companies from around the world.

texts: P/E of 70 or P/E of 9
Laura
I'm torn between a tech company with a P/E of 70 that's growing 40 % a year…
…and an insurer with a P/E of 9 growing 3 %. Which is better?
Which reasoning is right?
The P/E 70 one: it's growing much faster
If that growth is already in the price, any disappointment sinks it.
It depends whether the price reflects its future properly
Exactly. What matters is what you pay for what you get.
The P/E 9 one: it's cheap
It might be cheap for a reason: a stagnant business disappoints too.
Cheap is sometimes cheap for a reason: that's the **value trap**.
A great company isn't always a great investment: it depends on the price.
How many years of profits are you paying for?
This share costs **€100** and earns **€2 per share** a year. The **P/E** is the price ÷ earnings per share.
If earnings don't grow at all, how many years does it take to get the €100 back from profits?
About 5 years
About 20 years
50 years
P/E = 100 ÷ 2 = **50**: you're paying for 50 years of current earnings. The market expects a lot of growth.
Without touching the price, find how much earnings would need to grow to get it back in 15 years.
With a P/E of 50, you get the price back in 15 years only if earnings grow **16 % a year**, without fail. That's paying for **growth**: if it disappoints, a high P/E deflates in one go.
That growth is already in the price. What if it doesn't come?
More growth, fewer years to get back what you pay.
Raise the earnings growth
Growth or value?
Two styles: **growth**, where you pay today for future earnings, and **value**, where you buy current earnings at a discount.
Growth
Value
Its sales grow 40 % a year
It's growing fast: the market pays today for what it expects tomorrow.
P/E of 8 and a steady dividend
Cheap relative to what it earns today, and it pays out: value.
It reinvests everything and pays no dividend
It reinvests almost everything to keep growing.
A mature consumer goods company
A mature business: the classic value stock.
It trades cheaply relative to its net assets
Cheap relative to what it owns: value.
P/E of 50 thanks to a new product
Expensive relative to what it earns today: growth.
Sort the six companies.

Growth: **high P/E**, little dividend and lots of reinvestment; value: **low P/E**, mature business and dividend, and neither always wins. Try it: in Market, compare the chart of NVIDIA with that of Coca-Cola.
Hint: does it reinvest to grow or pay out what it earns?
Look at the P/E: high for growth, low for value.
Tap each company: growth or value?
Fewer shares, more profit
Leo
I own shares in a company that's going to buy back its own. What's in it for me?
A company earns 500 million and has 100 million shares: **€5 of earnings per share** (EPS).
It has announced it will buy back and cancel 10 million of its own shares.
What happens to earnings per share?
It rises: the same profit across fewer shares
That's it: 500 divided by 90 million, **€5.56**. 11 % more.
It falls: the company has spent money
The profit is the same, but it's shared among fewer shares: it rises.
It doesn't change: the profit is the same
The profit is, but there are fewer shares: each one gets more.
And me, when I haven't done anything?
Your percentage of the company goes up without you putting in a single euro.
Dividend or buyback?
Both return money to shareholders, but in different ways. What goes with each?
Dividend
Buyback
Money lands in your account
A dividend is paid in cash.
The number of shares goes down
Bought-back shares are cancelled: fewer are left.
You're taxed in the year you receive it
A dividend is taxed when you receive it.
You're only taxed when you sell
The gain builds up in the price and you pay when you sell.
Your percentage of the company goes up
Fewer shares in total: each one is a bigger slice.
The share drops on the ex-dividend date
That day the price drops by roughly the amount paid out.
Sort the six cards.
A **dividend** reaches you in cash and is taxed that year. A **buyback** increases your stake and you're only taxed when you sell.
Hint: a buyback doesn't pay anything into your account; it increases your stake.
Two ways to return money, with different tax treatment.
Tap each card: dividend or buyback?

steps.title: What price it buys back at
steps.body:
Apple has been buying back shares since 2012, to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars.

But buying back at a **high price** destroys value, and doing it **with debt** adds risk.
steps.key: A buyback shares the cake among fewer owners.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Apple, which has been buying back shares since 2012, and add it to your Favourites.

u8l2-2.prompt: Match each right with its type.
options: Voting on the board of directors
Buying before anyone else in a capital increase
u8l2-2.explanation: Economic, voting and information rights, plus pre-emptive rights so you don't lose your percentage.

u8l2-3.prompt: At the general meeting, how much does your vote normally weigh?
options: The same as a big fund's
According to what you paid for each share
According to the number of shares you hold
u8l2-3.explanation: As a general rule, one share = one vote. Whoever has more shares has more votes.

u8l2-7.prompt: Listed companies must report inside information to the ____ so that everyone learns about it at the same time.
u8l2-7.explanation: The Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores supervises the Spanish stock market and publishes that information for free.

options: Being able to buy new shares before others in a capital increase, so you don't lose your percentage
Voting twice at the general meeting
Getting the dividend before other shareholders
u8l2-8.explanation: If the company issues new shares, existing shareholders can buy first in proportion to what they hold.

u8l2-9.prompt: What can the general meeting of shareholders decide? Select all that apply.
options: Setting the share price on the stock market
u8l2-9.explanation: The price is set by the market through supply and demand, not by the meeting.

u8l2-11.prompt: The company Sara holds shares in announces a capital increase: it will issue new shares to raise money. Sara doesn't want to lose her percentage. What does she do?
options: She votes against it at the meeting and forgets about it
She uses her pre-emptive rights and buys the new shares she's entitled to
She does nothing: her shares are still hers
u8l2-11.explanation: That's what pre-emptive rights are for: buying what you're entitled to first so you don't lose your share. Doing nothing seems neutral, but with more shares in circulation your percentage falls.
feedback: Voting is her right, but if the capital increase is approved, she gets diluted anyway.
Good: she buys in proportion to what she already has and her percentage doesn't change.
They're still hers, but there will be more shares in total: her percentage falls. That's dilution.

u8l3-1.prompt: Put a dividend's dates in order.
u8l3-1.explanation: First it's announced; from the ex-dividend date the share trades without the right; then they check who the shareholders are (record) and finally it's paid.

u8l3-7.prompt: This is the share of a utility known for paying regular dividends. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u8l3-7.explanation: A company paying a dividend doesn't make its short-term price predictable: the dividend is part of the total return, not a guarantee.

u8l3-8.prompt: Bruno sees a share with a 14 % dividend and wants to put all his savings into it. What would you do in his shoes?
options: Buy right now, 14 % is a bargain
Look into why the price has fallen and whether profits cover the dividend
Buy just before the ex-dividend date, collect and sell
u8l3-8.explanation: Dividend yield rises when the price falls; sometimes it signals problems at the company.
feedback: If the market expects a cut, the dividend may drop and the price fall even further: the 14 % was an illusion.
Good: a dividend like that is often an alarm bell. If profits don't cover it, it'll probably be cut.
The price drops by roughly the dividend on the ex-dividend date and you pay tax on top: there's no free money.

u8l3-9.explanation: That's why, if the price falls, the dividend yield «rises» even though the company isn't paying any more.

u8l3-10.prompt: In Spain, what withholding is normally applied to dividends?
u8l3-10.explanation: The payer withholds 19 % on account of IRPF (Spanish income tax). Dividends then go into the savings tax base, taxed at 19 % to 30 %.

u8l4-5.prompt: Match each operation with what happens.
u8l4-5.explanation: Splits and reverse splits don't change the value of your position; capital increases and scrips do change the company's total number of shares.
right: New shares and new money for the company
You choose to be paid in cash or in new shares

u8l4-6.prompt: Why does a company usually do a split?
options: To make each share cheaper and more manageable
u8l4-6.explanation: No money comes in and the company's value doesn't change: only the price of each share falls.

u8l4-7.prompt: What happens to your percentage of the company?
options: Capital increase you don't take part in
Capital increase where you buy your full entitlement
u8l4-7.explanation: Only a capital increase you don't take part in dilutes you. If you exercise your pre-emptive rights, you keep your percentage.

u8l4-9.prompt: Quick: 2-for-1 split of an €80 share. New price?
u8l4-9.explanation: 80 ÷ 2 = €40, and you have twice as many shares.

u8l4-11.prompt: NVIDIA announces a 10×1 split and a friend tells you: «Now that each share costs ten times less, it's the time to buy». What do you reply?
options: That he should sell any he has before the split so as not to lose out
That the split doesn't change what the company is worth: you have to decide on the business and its total price
That he's right: it's much cheaper now
u8l4-11.explanation: A split changes the price of each share, not the value of the company. The temptation is to see a bargain in the lower price per share, but what you pay for the whole business hasn't changed.
feedback: There's nothing to lose: after the split, his money is worth the same.
Good: ten smaller slices of the same pizza are still the same pizza.
Each share costs less, but the company is worth the same: it isn't cheaper.

options: Yes: if you don't take part, your percentage of the company falls
No: your shares are still the same
Yes: they take away some of your shares
u8l4-12.explanation: In a capital increase new shares are issued: if you don't buy the ones you're entitled to, your percentage falls (dilution). It's tempting to think nothing happens because you keep your shares, but the total has grown.
feedback: That's it. There are more shares and you have the same ones: you get diluted.
The same shares, but of a pie with more slices: your share falls.
Nobody takes anything from you: what falls is your percentage.
lines: My company is going to raise capital with new shares.
I'm not planning to buy any. Does it affect me at all?

u8l5-2.prompt: Match each size with its approximate market cap (convention in dollars).
u8l5-2.explanation: These are rough ranges used by indices and fund managers; there's no single official cut-off.

u8l5-3.prompt: Match each index with what it measures.
u8l5-3.explanation: There are indices for every size: that way you can compare how they perform.

u8l5-4.prompt: What does a small company usually have compared with a giant?
options: More growth potential and more risk
u8l5-4.explanation: It can grow faster, but its price moves more and it goes bust more often.

u8l5-8.prompt: Quick: how is market cap calculated?
u8l5-8.explanation: It's the company's value on the stock market.

options: No, small caps never go up
Yes, in the long run they always win
They can return more, but with more risk, and it's not a fixed rule
u8l5-10.explanation: Size changes the risk profile, but it doesn't guarantee a result.
feedback: Some small caps become giants; the hard part is knowing which ones in advance.
Not always: there have been periods of many years in which large caps clearly beat them.
That's it! More potential, more scares and years when they do worse.
lines: Small caps go up more than large caps, right?
So I'm moving everything into small caps 🚀

u8l5-11.prompt: You want to invest in small US companies, but without betting everything on one. What do you do?
options: I buy a Russell 2000 ETF, which holds around 2,000 small caps
I buy the micro cap a forum recommends
I buy the small cap that has risen most this month
u8l5-11.explanation: A small-cap ETF gives you their potential without depending on just one. Picking a single one because it has risen or because of a forum is tempting, but it concentrates all the risk of bankruptcy.
feedback: Good: you get the potential of small caps, spread across many. If one goes bust, you barely notice.
A single tiny, illiquid company: if it goes wrong, you lose almost everything.
What has risen most isn't what will rise most, and you still have everything in a single company.

u8l6-1.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning.
u8l6-1.explanation: Two styles, a tool to measure them and a trap worth knowing about.
right: Cheap because the business is getting worse
You buy current earnings at a discount
You pay today for future earnings

u8l6-4.prompt: March 2000: the Nasdaq 100, packed with growth tech stocks, has multiplied more than 4 times since the end of 1997. What happened next?
u8l6-4.explanation: With sky-high P/Es, the price depends on very demanding expectations being met. It's a classic case for studying growth and valuation.

options: A cheap share that keeps falling because its business is deteriorating
A fund that charges hidden fees
u8l6-6.explanation: A low P/E may reflect that profits are about to fall: sometimes cheap is cheap for a reason.

u8l6-8.explanation: The P/E measures how many years of current earnings you're paying for.

u8l6-10.prompt: Which style suffers more if expected growth disappoints?
u8l6-10.explanation: With a high P/E, the price already reflects future earnings; if they don't arrive, the P/E deflates.

u8l7-1.prompt: What does a company do in a share buyback?
options: Buys its own shares and usually cancels them
u8l7-1.explanation: When they're cancelled, there are fewer shares and each one is worth a bigger part of the company.

u8l7-6.prompt: Match each use of profit with its effect.
u8l7-6.explanation: A company can pay out, buy back, reinvest or pay down debt: each option makes sense at a different moment.
right: Fewer shares and a bigger slice for each

u8l7-7.prompt: A company announces a big buyback funded by a loan, right when its share is at an all-time high with a very high P/E. How do you see it?
options: With caution: price and debt matter
u8l7-7.explanation: A buyback is only as good as the price it's done at and how it's paid for.
feedback: Buying back expensively and with debt can destroy value: it pays a lot for each share and adds risk.
Good: a buyback creates value if it's done at a good price and without putting the company at risk.
They're legal and common; in the US they've been subject to a 1 % tax since 2023.

u8l7-9.explanation: Net profit ÷ number of shares. A buyback raises it because the denominator falls.

u8l7-10.prompt: Why do some investors prefer buybacks to dividends?
options: Because they're not taxed until you sell
Because Hacienda (the Spanish tax office) pays for them
u8l7-10.explanation: A dividend is taxed when you receive it; with a buyback, your gain builds up in the price and you pay when you sell.
